about: Hand-written retrieval eval. Ten questions in an applicant's voice, each with the document(s) that should come back and verbatim text those documents actually contain. Keyed to source_id and text, never to chunk ids: chunk sizing is still tunable and every id would shift, which would break the eval silently. Every anchor was copied out of data/processed after grepping for it, not written from memory. Run scripts/eval_retrieval.py --validate to re-check that claim.

fields.expected: Documents a correct answer needs. Scored: recall is found/total, hit is any.
fields.anchors: Verbatim substrings of that document. Scored separately — coming back from the right chapter is weaker than coming back from the right paragraph.
fields.acceptable: Not wrong to return and not required. Excluded from the off-target count so that number means something.
fields.note: Why these documents and not others. The part that is judgment, kept next to the part that is mechanical.

questions.question: can I get a fee waiver for naturalization?

anchors: household income level is at or below 150 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines
receiving a means-tested benefit at the time of filing the request for fee waiver

questions.note: The one chapter that states the three grounds for a waiver. NWIRP is acceptable rather than expected on purpose: it enjoined the 2020 rule that would have gutted fee waivers, which is background an applicant might want and is not the answer to whether they qualify. It is also the 248-chunk document that crowds this question's top-5, so keeping it out of `expected` is what makes the crowding visible instead of scoring as success.

questions.question: I have a disability and cannot learn English. Is there an exception to the English test?

anchors: A licensed medical professional must complete a Medical Certification for Disability Exceptions (Form N-648)
disability or impairment that affects functioning such that the alien is unable to meet the English and civics requirements

questions.note: The N-648 chapter is the whole answer. Accommodations (Part C) is a different thing that sounds like the same thing — a wheelchair or a sign-language interpreter at the interview, not an exemption from the requirement — so it is acceptable and not expected. De Dandrade and Moya are the litigation over N-648 denials.

questions.question: I am 68 and have had a green card for 22 years. Do I still have to take the English test?

anchors: The alien is age 50 or older at the time of filing for naturalization and has lived as an LPR in the United States for at least 20 years
An alien receives special consideration in the civics test if, at the time of filing the application, the alien is 65 years of age or older

questions.note: Two anchors because the answer is split: at 50/20 the English test is waived outright, at 65/20 the civics test additionally gets a shorter form. A retrieval that finds one and not the other gives a half answer, which is exactly what the anchor metric is for. The question states facts rather than the rule, so nothing in it lexically matches `age 50 or older` — a deliberate test of the embedding rather than of keyword overlap.

questions.question: I was outside the United States for eight months. Does that break my continuous residence?

anchors: absent from the United States for more than 6 months but less than 1 year
may overcome the presumption of a break in the continuity of residence by providing evidence

questions.note: Eight months falls in the rebuttable band, so the useful answer is the presumption plus the fact that it can be overcome — hence the second anchor. Physical presence (D.4) is a separate requirement the same trip also affects, so it is acceptable; answering only D.4 would be answering a question that was not asked.

questions.question: USCIS interviewed me over a year ago and still has not decided my case. What can I do?

anchors: USCIS has 120 days from the date of the initial naturalization interview to issue a decision
an applicant may request judicial review of his or her application in district court
that court has exclusive jurisdiction over the naturalization application unless and until the matter is remanded to the agency

questions.note: The only question whose `expected` spans both halves, and the reason it is here: the statutory clock is USCIS policy, but what a court can actually do once you sue is a holding that appears nowhere in the Policy Manual. Aljabri is the expected case because it is the exclusive-jurisdiction holding the other delay cases cite; the six other delay opinions are acceptable, not required, since any of them answers the question adequately.

questions.question: My naturalization application was denied. Can I appeal it?

anchors: A naturalization applicant may request judicial review before a United States district court of his or her denied naturalization application
The district court reviews the case de novo and makes its own findings of fact and conclusions of law

questions.note: B.6 covers both steps in order — the N-336 hearing before USCIS, then district court review — and the ordering is the part applicants get wrong, so it is the expected document. The procedural opinions are all about what happens when someone skips or misuses a step; useful, not the answer. Iqbal was added to `acceptable` after the first run put four of its chunks in the top 5: it walks through the administrative appeal under 1447(a) and does answer the question, so counting it off-target was wrong. B.6 not ranking at all is the real failure and is unaffected.

questions.question: How long do I have to be married to a U.S. citizen before I can apply for citizenship?

anchors: must have lived in marital union with his or her citizen spouse for at least those 3 years
Physically present in the United States for at least 18 months (548 days) out of the 3 years

questions.note: The literal answer is three years, and the trap is that the three years are three separate requirements at once — married, resident, present — which is why the second anchor is the 18-month one. G.2 defines living in marital union and is acceptable; on its own it never states the period.

questions.question: I gave a wrong answer at my interview. Can that count against my good moral character?

anchors: False testimony occurs when the alien deliberately intends to deceive the U.S. Government while under oath in order to obtain an immigration benefit
False statements in a written application and falsified documents, whether or not under oath, do not constitute
Kariuki claimed under oath that he never had falsely represented himself

questions.note: Asked the way an applicant would ask it — nobody types `false testimony`, they type `wrong answer` — so this is the sharpest vocabulary-gap test in the set. The second anchor is the answer to the question actually asked: a wrong answer on the form is not testimony, an oral one under oath is. Kariuki is expected because it is the case where the wrong answer was repeated aloud and that repetition was the whole holding. Yemer was added to `acceptable` after the first run: it discusses false testimony eight times, so it is a fair thing to return. Hassan, which also ranked, mentions it zero times and stays off-target.

questions.question: Can I still naturalize if I am in removal proceedings?

anchors: USCIS may not consider the merits of any application for naturalization for an applicant in removal proceedings
USCIS lacks the authority to grant naturalization to an applicant against whom there is a pending removal proceeding initiated by a warrant of arrest
the limitation imposed by § 1429 applies only to the executive branch

questions.note: Expected was 12 B.4 until the first run returned 12 D.2 at rank 1 with the section heading `F. Removal Proceedings > 2. Pending Removal Proceedings`. D.2 is the eligibility chapter and has a section on exactly this; B.4 states the same rule from the denial side. Requiring both would be requiring redundancy, so D.2 is expected and B.4 moved to acceptable — logged because relaxing a key after seeing the score is the direction that flatters the system, and this one was checked by reading D.2 rather than by watching the number. The two halves are also less opposed than first written: D.2 cites Yith in a footnote and confines it to the 9th Circuit, so the policy manual reports the split rather than ignoring it. Yith stays expected — an answer built only from the policy side tells a 9th Circuit applicant the wrong thing.

questions.question: Will two DUI convictions stop me from becoming a citizen?

anchors: Evidence of two or more DUI convictions during the statutory period establishes a rebuttable presumption that an alien lacks GMC
the alien may be able to later naturalize if able to establish good moral character

questions.note: The first anchor was originally the Markdown table row listing DUI as a conditional bar, on the theory that this question doubles as a check that table text survived the chunker. It does survive — validation finds it in one chunk — but it never ranks, and the substantive DUI section does, so the anchor moved to the prose. A summary table row embeds as a citation list with no sentence in it; presence in the index is not the same as reachability by a question, and that is validation's job rather than this metric's. The second anchor is the word `conditional` doing its work: two DUIs are a bar for a period, not forever, and an answer that omits that is wrong in the direction that matters to the person asking.
